input.task:
The month-end export from the finance system (made by Excel, CRLF line ends, starting with a UTF-8 byte-order mark) gives wrong report numbers.
- The column "Region" is not found, because the header starts with the byte-order mark. Regions show up twice ("East" and "East\r"). Notes that contain a comma or a line break create bogus extra rows.
- Reading must follow RFC 4180. A field may be quoted; inside quotes a comma or a line break (LF or CRLF) is data and is kept exactly, and "" stands for one quote. A quote in the middle of an unquoted field is an ordinary character, and a quote that is never closed is an error. A line ends with LF or CRLF. A blank line (nothing between two line ends) is skipped, and the last line may lack its line end. A byte-order mark at the start is not part of the first field.
- With summarizeChunks the result depends on where the chunks end. createParser().write(chunk) must return the same rows however the text is cut, even between CR and LF, or between the two quotes of "". end() must report a quote that was never closed.
- Amounts: "1,234.50" counts as 1 and "(12.00)" is ignored. An amount is an optional + or -, an optional $, € or £, digits (with commas only as thousands separators in groups of three), and an optional fraction; ".5" is fine. An amount in parentheses is negative. Anything else, "1,23" included, is not an amount.
- In a group, count is every row, but sum, avg, min and max use only the rows that have an amount. avg is the sum divided by the number of those rows; avg, min and max are null when there are none, and sum is then 0. Sums must be exact decimals (ten times 0.1 is 1, not 0.9999999999999999).
- Group keys are trimmed but stay case-sensitive. Column names in the options match the header ignoring case and the spaces around names, and toRecords trims header names too. A row shorter than the header gets blank fields; fields beyond the header are ignored.

summarize, summarizeChunks, renderTable, parseCsv, createParser, toRecords and toNumber keep their names, signatures and result shapes. The existing tests must keep passing and must not be edited; put any new tests in new files.

tier.name: hard
tier.basis: RFC 4180 reader that must give the same rows however the text is split, plus exact decimal sums and amount parsing; reference rewrites about 250 lines in 5 files. Near the top of the tier.

input.task:
We added yen and Kuwaiti dinar accounts and the books stopped adding up. Moving money between a USD account and a JPY account gives amounts that are off by a factor of 100, and USD to KWD is off by a factor of 10. Between two-decimal currencies, converted amounts are sometimes one cent away from our spreadsheet, mostly for negative amounts, for exact half-cent cases and for cross rates that go through USD. Splitting a payment between three people leaves one cent unassigned. Our net worth figure changes with the number of accounts the money is spread over. A small negative amount on a statement loses its minus sign (-0.05 prints as 0.05). Percentage fees come out a unit short whenever the exact fee is half a unit or more.

The rules we agreed on: money is integer minor units and never goes through binary floating point. Rounding is half away from zero, and it happens once, on the final value, never on an intermediate one. A split gives away exactly the amount it is given: each payee gets the rounded-down share, the leftover units go one each to the largest remainders, the earlier payee wins a tie, and the weights must be non-negative integers that add up to more than zero. A negative total is split like its absolute value, and each share then gets the minus sign (so -100 over three equal weights gives -34, -33, -33). Net worth converts the total of each currency once, rounds each converted total like any other conversion, then adds them. rate() must keep returning a plain number, and the public exports stay as they are. The existing tests must keep passing and must not be edited; put any new tests in new files.

tier.name: hard
tier.basis: Money rounding and allocation across 6 of 11 files; reference rewrites about 240 lines. About 8 min to read, then 7 rules to restore with a re-check of the arithmetic.

input.task:
Clients and operators report several problems with the rate limiter.
- A client that polls every 400 ms against a limit of one request per second is never let in, while one that polls every 600 ms gets in early. A token must be available exactly when enough time has passed: at 1.5 tokens per second the next token comes after 667 ms, not after 666. Progress between two calls must not be lost.
- A refused request must not use up tokens, since retries then make the wait longer. retryAfterMs is the exact wait in milliseconds, rounded up: 0 when the request is allowed and at least 1 when it is refused. A request whose cost is more than the burst can never pass: retryAfterMs is null and nothing is spent. A cost that is not a whole number of at least 1 is a RangeError.
- One busy user locks out everyone else on the same rule. Every key must have its own bucket, and a new key starts with a full one.
- When several rules match a key, the most specific wins: the exact key, then the longest prefix, then '*'. Between equal matches the rule listed first wins.
- maxKeys is ignored and memory grows. When a new key arrives and the limiter holds maxKeys keys, it first drops every key whose bucket has filled up again (it is as good as new), and if that is not enough it drops the least recently used keys. A key is used whenever it is checked, whether the request is allowed or not.
- remaining counts whole tokens. The headers ratelimit-reset and retry-after are whole seconds, rounded up; retry-after is at least 1 and is left out when the request can never pass.
- After a system clock was set back, clients got free tokens. A clock that moves back must add nothing, and time that was already counted must not be counted again.

We are moving the token arithmetic from floating point to integers (perSecond has at most three decimals). The exports of index.mjs and the shape of the check() result must stay exactly as they are. The existing tests must keep passing and must not be edited; put any new tests in new files.

tier.name: hard
tier.basis: Token bucket moved from floats to integers with per-key buckets, rule priority, LRU eviction and clock rollback; reference is about 155 lines in 5 files. Several rules interact.

input.task: Our email and page templates render wrong in a few cases. - A value with an apostrophe breaks out of attributes written with single quotes: with t = it's. The apostrophe must be escaped as ' like the other special characters. - A partial used without an argument inside {{#each}} shows data from the page instead of the current item. Without an argument a partial gets the current context, whatever block it is used in, and ../ inside a partial means the same as at the place where the partial is used. - A partial that is a function (partials: { badge: (ctx) => '' + ctx.n + '' }) comes out escaped, as text. Partials are the template author's own markup, whether they are template strings or functions, and are written out as they are. - Inside {{#each items}}, {{#if show}}{{../title}}{{/if}} prints nothing. ../ must still reach the context outside the loop, because {{#if}} and {{#unless}} do not change the context and do not add a level. - In nested loops, the {{@index}} of the outer loop is wrong after the inner loop has run. Each loop must keep its own @index, @key, @first and @last. - {{#if list}} renders its body for an empty list. False values are false, null, undefined, 0, NaN, the empty string and the empty array. Everything else, an empty object included, is true. The existing tests must keep passing and must not be edited; put any new tests in new files.

tier.name: hard
tier.basis: Six separate bugs in a 294-line template engine of 13 files; reference rewrites about 130 lines in 4 files. About 6 min to read the code and 2 to 3 min per bug.

input.task:
The cache behaves oddly under load.
- ttl: '30s' lasts 30 milliseconds. Durations written as text must be converted to milliseconds ('500ms', '30s', '5m', '2h', '1d', '1.5s', '1h30m'); a number is milliseconds, and text without a unit (such as '5') is an error.
- An entry set at time 0 with a ttl of 100 is still returned at time 100. It must expire exactly at set time + ttl, for get, has, peek, ttlOf, keys, size and bytes alike. ttlOf must answer in milliseconds (Infinity when the entry never expires).
- With maxBytes, setting the same key again a few times makes the cache evict everything.
- Expired entries still count towards maxBytes and push live entries out. Expired entries must go before any live entry is evicted (an expired entry that goes counts as an expiration, never as an eviction), and size() and bytes() never count them.
- A value that is bigger than maxBytes by itself wipes the whole cache. It must not be stored (set returns false), nothing else is evicted for it, and an older value under the same key is removed (that removal is not an eviction and does not count in the stats).
- has() and peek() change the recency order and the hit and miss statistics. Only get() may.
- The default size of a string must be its UTF-8 length in bytes.
- getOrLoad: after a loader has failed once, every later call for that key rejects with the same error. A failed load must not be remembered: callers that were waiting for it all get the rejection, and the next call tries again. The existing tests must keep passing and must not be edited; put any new tests in new files. The public exports stay as they are.

tier.name: hard
tier.basis: Seven cache faults (units, expiry edges, byte accounting, eviction order, stats, async loader) across 14 files; reference rewrites about 220 lines in 5 files.

input.task:
Our access-policy evaluator lets people do things they should not, and refuses other things.
- A user who holds a role with an allow statement and a role with a deny statement for the same request is allowed when the allow statement was added first. explain() names only one statement, and a statement for two roles is named twice.
- A role cycle that runs through other roles (a, then b, then c, then a again) is accepted.
- After a role gets other parents, or a group gets other roles, users keep their old permissions until their own record is set again.
- A user who has direct roles loses the roles of their groups.
- A statement for /projects/4 also covers /projects/42, and /a/**/z does not cover /a/z.
- With a statement for /homes/${user.id}, a user whose id is * can read every home folder, and an id with a slash in it reaches folders it should not.
- A statement with notActions acts as if the actions were a plain list.
- A deny statement with a condition on an attribute that the user does not have has no effect. A between condition still holds at its end time.
- Adding a statement with an id that exists silently adds a second one, and a removed statement keeps applying.
- A request for a user that does not exist crashes with a TypeError.

The rules we agreed on:
- Nothing is allowed unless a statement allows it. Any applying deny statement beats every applying allow statement. explain() gives { allowed, decision, by }: decision is 'deny', 'allow' or 'default', and by holds the ids of every applying statement of the winning effect, once each, sorted by id (empty for 'default').
- A role inherits the statements of its parents and of their parents, and so on, deny statements included. A role cannot inherit from itself, directly or through other roles: defineRole() throws CycleError and the roles stay as they were. A user's roles are their own roles together with the roles of their groups, with everything those inherit. Every change to roles, groups, users and statements counts from the next request.
- A statement for the role '*' applies to every known user. A user that is not known is denied with decision 'default'; it is not an error. An action that is not 'namespace:name', or a resource that is not an absolute path, is a PolicyError even then.
- A resource path is cut into segments; empty segments are dropped, so '/a//b/' is '/a/b'. A '.' or '..' segment is a PolicyError, in a request and in a pattern. A pattern covers the resource it names and everything below it, compared segment by segment ('/projects/4' does not cover '/projects/42'), unless the statement has exact: true. In a pattern, '*' is exactly one segment and '**' is zero or more segments. The segment ${user.id}, as a whole segment, means exactly the id of the user who asks, as one literal segment, whatever characters that id holds (an id with a slash matches no segment). ${ inside a longer segment is a PolicyError.
- Actions: '*' matches every action, 'namespace:*' matches every action of that namespace, anything else matches only itself. A statement with notActions applies to every action except those listed.
- Conditions of a statement must all hold. owner: true holds when context.owner is the id of the user. mfa: true holds when context.mfa is true. attrs holds when each listed attribute of the user is strictly equal to the given value. between: [from, to] holds from 'from' up to, but not including, 'to' of the policy clock. If an attribute that a condition needs is missing (no context.owner, no context.mfa, no such user attribute), the condition cannot be told: in a deny statement it counts as holding, in an allow statement as not holding. A condition that fails for sure settles the statement, whatever else is missing.
- A statement id must be unique (PolicyError); removeStatement(id) removes the statement at once and answers true, or false when there is none, and the id is free again.

Public exports stay as they are. The existing tests must keep passing and must not be edited; put any new tests in new files.

tier.basis: Estimate from the size of the work, not a timed solve: about 15 separate faults in 9 of 13 files, roughly 25 minutes to find them by reading and probing the evaluator and 30 to fix and check them.

input.task:
Our stock holds (reservations) are wrong in several ways.
- After a hold's time is up, its stock stays reserved until someone makes another hold: the stock numbers still show it as held, and adjust() refuses a correction that the shelf can take.
- A hold is still alive at the exact moment it should expire.
- commit(), extend() and release() work on a hold whose time is up, and commit() then takes stock that may be promised to someone else.
- A hold can be extended again and again with no end, and a long ttlMs gives a hold a longer life than the shop allows.
- Two lines of one request for the same sku are each checked alone, so a hold can take more than is on the shelf and the available number goes negative.
- The reply for a request that cannot be served names only the first short line.
- Sending a hold again with the same id but another quantity is taken for a replay, and an id can never be used again after its hold was released or expired.
- The available number goes below 0 when the safety stock is more than what is on the shelf.
- expiring() puts the holds in the order of their ids.

The rules we agreed on:
- A hold is active from the moment it is made up to, but not including, its expiresAt. Expired holds count nowhere: not in snapshot(), not in the check of a new hold, not in adjust(), not in expiring(), and commit(), extend() and release() answer false for them.
- The first expiresAt is now + min(ttlMs, maxHoldMs); ttlMs is whole milliseconds of at least 1 (RangeError otherwise). extend(id, ms) adds ms to the current expiresAt, but a hold never lives longer than maxHoldMs counted from its creation; when the extension is cut short it still answers true. ms must be a whole number of at least 1 (RangeError otherwise).
- The lines of a request are merged first: one line per sku, quantities added up, sorted by sku. A hold takes all its lines or nothing. When it cannot be served the reply is { ok: false, short } and short holds an item { sku, wanted, available } for every sku that is short, sorted by sku, where wanted is the merged quantity.
- available is onHand - held - safety[sku], and never below 0.
- A hold id that is active with the same merged lines is a replay: the reply is { ok: true, replay: true } with the existing hold, and nothing is reserved twice or renewed. The same id active with other lines or other quantities throws ConflictError. An id of a committed hold throws ConflictError for good. An id of a released or an expired hold is free and starts a new hold.
- adjust() takes a whole, non-zero delta; a delta that would leave less on the shelf than the active holds need throws ConflictError, and an unknown sku throws UnknownSkuError.
- expiring(withinMs) lists { id, expiresAt } of the active holds that end within withinMs from now (an end exactly withinMs away counts), soonest first, ties by id.

Public exports stay as they are. The existing tests must keep passing and must not be edited; put any new tests in new files.

input.task:
Our invoice calculator gives totals that do not add up and amounts that differ by a cent.
- Quantities with too many decimals, or written as 1e2 or true, are accepted. Some amounts too big for a whole number do not give an error and the result is wrong.
- Small amounts such as 5 cents or 0 are written without a leading 0 in the whole part. A calendar date that does not exist (the 30th of February) is accepted for a service period.
- When the invoice is set to round half to even, percentage discounts and tax on prices that include tax still round half up. An unknown rounding or tax mode is silently replaced by the default, and cash rounding is accepted for euros.
- A fixed discount on a line can be larger than the line. The invoice discount is not given when the sum of the lines is exactly the minimum, a cap is ignored for a percentage, and lines that must not be discounted still count and still get a share of it. When the discount cannot be shared evenly, the extra cent goes to a later line.
- The tax does not take the invoice discount into account, so net, tax and total do not match. For prices that include tax, a half-cent tie gives a different tax than the net amount does. The tax mode that rounds once for each rate behaves like the line mode.
- A service line that starts before its period, ends after it, or is not served at all gives the wrong amount.
- A credit note for the last part of a line does not take exactly what is left, so the credit notes of one line do not add up to the line. The same line can be returned twice in one credit note.

The rules we agreed on:
- Amounts are whole numbers of the smallest currency unit. Every input amount and every computed value must be a safe whole number (Number.isSafeInteger), else InvoiceError; this includes formatMoney, roundDiv and allocate. Currencies are USD, EUR, GBP and CHF (2 decimals), JPY (0) and KWD (3), written exactly like that; anything else is an InvoiceError.
- roundDiv(n, d, mode) with d a safe whole number above 0 rounds n/d with integers; a tie goes away from zero for 'half-up' and to the even number for 'half-even'; also for a negative n. Any other mode is an InvoiceError.
- The rounding of the invoice is 'half-up' (the default when it is not given) or 'half-even'; any other value is an InvoiceError. It applies to every rounding of the invoice: the amount of a line, a percentage discount on a line and on the invoice, tax, a service period, and the part of a credit note. It does not apply to sharing a discount or tax over lines, and not to cash rounding. taxMode is 'line' (the default) or 'invoice', else InvoiceError. pricesIncludeTax and cashRounding are true or false, else InvoiceError.
- A line has unitPrice (a whole number, 0 or more), quantity, tax and optional discountable (true or false, default true), discount and service. A quantity is a number or a string of digits with up to 3 decimals ('1.5', 2, '0.001'), above 0, else InvoiceError. The amount of a line is unitPrice times quantity, rounded once. The tax of a line is the name of an entry of taxRates, which must be an own name of that object; a rate is a whole number of basis points from 0 to 10000 (1900 is 19%). An unknown tax name, an empty list of lines and a bad currency are InvoiceError.
- A discount is { percentBp } with a whole number from 0 to 10000, or { amount } with a whole number of 0 or more, never both and never neither; else InvoiceError. A line discount is taken from the amount of its line, and a fixed one is never more than that amount.
- The invoice discount is { percentBp } or { amount }, with optional minSubtotal (a whole number of 0 or more, default 0) and cap (a whole number of 0 or more). It is worked out on the sum of the amounts of the discountable lines after their own discounts. When that sum is below minSubtotal there is no discount (equal is enough). A percentage is rounded; a fixed amount is never more than the sum; cap limits the discount in both cases. Lines with discountable: false take no share. The discount is shared over the discountable lines in proportion to their amounts so that the shares add up to the discount exactly: whole numbers by the largest remainder method, equal remainders go to the lower line.
- allocate(total, weights) does that sharing: total is 0 or more, weights are whole numbers of 0 or more; all weights 0 is only allowed with a total of 0 (and no weights too); else InvoiceError.
- The order of work is: amount of every line, line discounts, invoice discount, tax. Tax is worked out on the amount left after both discounts. With prices without tax, tax is amount times rate over 10000, rounded, and total is net plus tax. With prices that include tax, net is amount times 10000 over (10000 plus rate), rounded, and tax is the amount minus net.
- taxMode 'line' rounds every line on its own. taxMode 'invoice' adds up the amounts of the lines with the same rate, works out the tax of that sum once, and shares that tax over those lines in proportion to their amounts by the same largest remainder method. The invoice has subtotal (sum of line amounts), discount (all discounts), net, tax, total (net plus tax, or the sum of amounts left when prices include tax), and taxes: one entry { rate, taxable, tax } for each rate in use, lowest rate first; categories with the same rate are one entry.
- A service line has service: { periodStart, periodEnd, from, to }, an object in which periodStart and periodEnd are required. The dates are real YYYY-MM-DD dates (also 29 February in a leap year), from and to are optional, and the period must not end before it starts; else InvoiceError. The line is charged for the days of the period it was served, both ends included: from the later of from and periodStart to the earlier of to and periodEnd. No served day gives 0. The amount is unitPrice times quantity times served days over the days of the period, rounded once.
- With cashRounding the invoice has due: the total rounded to the nearest 5 minor units, a tie going up, and rounding = due minus total. Only CHF has cash rounding; for any other currency it is an InvoiceError. Without it due is the total and rounding is 0.
- creditNote(invoice, returns, earlier) credits a returned quantity of lines: returns is a non-empty list of { line (an index of the invoice), quantity }, every line at most once. The part of a line is its net and its tax in proportion to the returned quantity, rounded with the rounding of the invoice, and never more than what is left. When the whole rest of the quantity of a line is returned, the credit is exactly the net and tax that are left, after the credit notes in earlier. A quantity above what is left, an unknown line, a bad quantity or a line twice is an InvoiceError.
- formatMoney(minor, currency) writes the amount with the decimals of the currency, a leading 0 in the whole part, commas for thousands, and a minus sign for a negative amount (never for zero), for example 0.05, -0.05, 1,234.50, 1,234 (JPY) and 0.005 (KWD).

Public exports stay as they are. The existing tests must keep passing and must not be edited; put any new tests in new files.

Roughly 35 minutes to find them and 25 to fix and check them.

input.task:
Our job queue misbehaves in production.
- After a handler throws, the queue stops starting jobs. With concurrency 2, three failing jobs leave it idle for good.
- A job that fails every time runs one time more than its maxAttempts. The first retry waits twice the configured base time. Waits such as 22.5 ms are cut to 22 instead of being rounded up.
- Errors we mark as not retryable are retried anyway, and the retryAfterMs that a rate-limited API puts on its error is ignored.
- With a dozen jobs of the same priority, the job enqueued tenth starts before the job enqueued second.
- A job whose name has no registered handler is started anyway, fails, and uses up its attempts.
- The same idempotency key sent for two different job names is treated as one job. A key is held forever, even after its job died, so the caller can never submit it again. Duplicate submissions show up as new jobs in stats().
- cancel() accepts jobs that already finished, and that frees their key.
- retryDead() puts a job back, but the job dies again after its first failure.
- Changing the object that enqueue() or get() returned changes the queue's own record.

The rules we agreed on:
- maxAttempts is the total number of runs, the first one included. The wait before retry n (n is 1 for the first retry) is baseMs * factor^(n-1), rounded up to a whole millisecond and never above capMs.
- An error whose retryable is exactly false ends the job at once (state dead). If the error has a retryAfterMs that is a finite number of 0 or more, the retry waits exactly that long and the cap does not apply to it; any other value of retryAfterMs is ignored. Such a retry still uses up an attempt.
- Jobs start by higher priority first, then the job that became due first (runAt), then the one enqueued first.
- A job without a registered handler stays queued, is not counted as an attempt and does not take a slot; it runs once a handler is registered.
- An idempotency key belongs to a job name together with the key. It is held while the job is queued (also while it waits for a retry) or running, and for keyTtlMs after the job finished with success, counted from the time it finished. A dead job or a cancelled job gives its key back at once. A duplicate submission returns a copy of the held job, counts in stats().duplicates and does not count in stats().enqueued.
- cancel(id) works only on a queued job (waiting, delayed, or waiting for a retry) and returns true; for any other job, or an unknown id, it returns false and changes nothing.
- retryDead(id) works only on a dead job: it becomes queued and due now, with attempts 0 and finishedAt null, and the call returns true; otherwise false.
- enqueue(), get(), the job given to a handler and the events all hand out copies, results included.

Public exports stay as they are. The existing tests must keep passing and must not be edited; put any new tests in new files.

input.task:
Our support SLA timer gives wrong deadlines and wrong flags.
- A calendar that is ahead of UTC (an office at +05:30, for example) opens and closes at the wrong hours, and the holiday and weekday checks are off for it.
- Some calendar setups that should work are refused (an offset of +14:00, two windows that touch), and some that should be refused are accepted (a time like 09:75, a weekday key such as 7).
- A special day with no windows does not close the day. Asking for the next opening at the exact closing time of a window gives that closing time.
- Time that runs out exactly at the end of a window is moved to the next opening. Asking for the business time between two instants in the wrong order gives 0.
- Events at the same instant (a pause and a resume together) are refused. A stop while paused adds the paused time to the elapsed time.
- A ticket that used exactly its target is marked as breached. The warning flag turns on too late, or not at all, at the exact level, and its result depends on rounding.
- Once the target is passed, a running clock fails with an error instead of keeping the deadline. A paused clock gets a deadline as if it was running.
- The response clock stops for pauses, and a stop in the history can make it fail. A priority that names a calendar called toString or constructor is accepted.

The rules we agreed on:
- A calendar has an offset in minutes ahead of UTC: a whole number from -720 to 840. Hours, weekdays, holidays and special days are all those of the local date. A calendar never changes its offset (no daylight saving).
- week has the keys 0 to 6 (0 is Sunday); any other key is refused with CalendarError. A weekday that is not listed is closed. A window is [start, end] as HH:MM. Minutes are 00 to 59, hours are 00 to 24, and 24:00 is the end of the day. The end must be after the start. Windows in one list may touch (12:00 end, 12:00 start) but not overlap, and the list may be in any order. Dates are real YYYY-MM-DD dates. Holidays are closed all day. A special day replaces the weekly windows of its date, and an empty list closes the day. A date that is a holiday and a special day is refused. A bad calendar throws CalendarError.
- The end of a window is closed and its start is open. nextOpen(calendar, ms) is ms itself when it is open, else the next start of a window. It looks ahead 3660 days, then throws CalendarError; so does addBusinessTime on a calendar that is never open.
- addBusinessTime(calendar, start, duration): the duration is a whole number of ms, 0 or more, else RangeError. 0 gives start. Closed time does not count. When the duration is used up exactly at the end of a window, the answer is that end.
- businessTimeBetween(calendar, from, to) is the open time in ms between them; it throws RangeError when to is before from.
- An event history starts with a start. After a start or a resume only a pause or a stop may follow; after a pause only a resume or a stop; nothing follows a stop. Events may have the same time, times may not go back, and now may not be before the last event; the order of the list is kept. A stop while paused adds no time. Any other fault is a SlaError.
- computeSla: target is a whole number of ms, 1 or more; warnPercent is above 0 and at most 100 (default 80); both are SlaError otherwise. The clock runs from a start or resume to the next pause or stop, or to now. A ticket is breached when the elapsed open time is more than the target (equal is on time). It is at risk when it is not breached and elapsed times 100 is at least target times warnPercent, tested exactly. remaining is target minus elapsed.
- deadline is the instant at which the elapsed time reached the target, also when that is in the past. If it has not been reached it is null for a paused or stopped clock, and for a running clock it is the instant ahead at which the target will be reached.
- A policy rule names a calendar and gives response and resolution targets. The response clock runs from createdAt to firstResponseAt (or to now) and pauses do not stop it. The resolution clock follows the events as they are. Only own names count: an unknown priority, or a rule that names an unknown calendar (also at creation), is a SlaError, whatever the name, toString included.

input.task:
Our text-table renderer breaks on real data.
- Korean, Japanese kana, full-width letters and emoji make the columns drift, and accented letters written as a letter plus a combining mark are counted twice. A family emoji (several people joined together), a flag and an emoji with a skin tone each count as several characters.
- Coloured text (ESC [ 31 m and the like) is counted as if the codes were visible, and a cut can fall inside a code or drop the code that switches the colour off.
- A tab shows as one space, null shows as the word null, an object shows as [object Object], and a lone carriage return or other control character is left in the cell.
- With the ellipsis '...' a cut cell is two columns too wide. A cut can split an accented letter or an emoji.
- A number such as 1.005 with 2 decimals gives 1.00, thousands separators also appear inside the decimals, -0.001 prints as -0.00, and decimals: 1.5 is accepted.
- Wrapped text loses its indent and any run of more than one space.
- Centred text puts the extra space on the left.
- The title of a wrapping column is cut instead of wrapped, a row is only as tall as its first cell, and a table without borders keeps trailing spaces.
- When maxWidth is set, the leftmost of the widest columns shrinks, columns with a fixed width shrink too, and minWidth is ignored.

The rules we agreed on:
- Width in terminal columns: a control character (below U+0020, and U+007F-009F) and a zero-width character (U+0300-036F, 1AB0-1AFF, 1DC0-1DFF, 200B-200F, 2060, 20D0-20FF, FE00-FE0F, FE20-FE2F: combining marks, zero-width space and joiners, variation selectors) take 0. Characters in these ranges take 2: Hangul jamo and syllables, CJK and kana and full-width forms, the ideographic space, regional indicators, and emoji blocks (U+1100-115F, 2E80-303E, 3041-33FF, 3400-4DBF, 4E00-9FFF, A000-A4CF, AC00-D7A3, F900-FAFF, FE30-FE6F, FF00-FF60, FFE0-FFE6, 1F1E6-1F1FF, 1F300-1F64F, 1F680-1F6FF, 1F900-1F9FF, 20000-3FFFD). All others take 1. Text is split into grapheme clusters, and a cluster takes the width of its widest character, but 2 if it holds U+FE0F. Width is counted per cluster everywhere: in widths, padding, cutting and wrapping.
- Colour codes are ESC [ digits and semicolons m. They take 0 columns and are never split. Any other control character, ESC alone included, is removed from a cell.
- A cell value is text as it is; null and undefined are empty; Date is its ISO string; an object or array is JSON; anything else is String(value). A cell with several lines (a new line, CRLF or a lone CR is a line break) is several lines. A tab moves to the next multiple of 4 columns counted from the start of its line.
- truncate(line, width, ellipsis) leaves a line that fits as it is. Otherwise it keeps as many whole clusters as fit in width minus the width of the ellipsis, then the ellipsis; the ellipsis is left out when it is wider than width. A cluster that does not fit whole is dropped. Colour codes found after the cut are kept, in order, after the ellipsis. Codes before the cut stay where they are.
- formatNumber(value, { decimals, thousands }) rounds half away from zero on the decimal digits of the number as JavaScript writes it (1.005 gives 1.01 at 2 decimals, -2.5 gives -3 at 0), never in exponent form. Thousands separators go in the whole part only. A result that is zero has no minus sign. decimals is a whole number from 0 to 20, else RangeError. NaN, Infinity and values that are not numbers are written with String().
- wrapLine(line, width) breaks at spaces. The spaces at a break are dropped, trailing spaces are dropped, the spaces inside a line stay as they are, and so does the indent of the first line. A word wider than width is cut into pieces of whole clusters. An empty line gives [''].
- Centring puts the extra space on the right. A row is as tall as its tallest cell (also the header row); shorter cells are filled with blank lines. Header cells follow the overflow rule of their column. With border: 'none' the trailing spaces of every line are removed.
- Column widths: width fixes a column. Otherwise it starts at its widest line (cells and title) and is held between minWidth (default 1) and maxWidth. If the table is wider than maxWidth (borders and padding count), the widest column that may shrink loses one column at a time, the rightmost of equally wide ones first, never below its minWidth and never a column with a fixed width. If that is not enough the table throws RangeError.

input.task:
Our URL router answers wrong in many small ways.
- GET /users/me goes to the /users/:id route although a /users/me route exists. In general the less specific route wins when two routes fit. A typed parameter such as :id<int> loses against a plain :id registered before it, and :id<int> accepts -5 and +5.
- /files/** matches /files with an empty rest.
- /tag/a%2Fb is a 404: the encoded slash splits the segment. %2541 comes out as A, and a + in the path comes out as a space.
- /x/./y and /x/z/../y are not the same as /x/y.
- A path with a broken escape such as /tag/%zz crashes with a URIError.
- In the query string only the last value of a repeated key is kept, a + stays a plus, c=1=2 is cut after the first equal sign, a key like __proto__ is lost, and a broken escape in the query crashes the request.
- With the redirect policy, every path with a trailing slash is redirected, also unknown ones, and the query string is lost.
- HEAD on a GET route is a 405. The allowed methods in a 405 come in registration order and miss HEAD and OPTIONS. GET /users/me is a 405 when only POST /users/me is registered and GET /users/:id covers it.
- A route added with a lowercase method such as 'get' is never found.
- Two routes that differ only in the name of a parameter are both accepted, a name can be used twice in one pattern, and an optional parameter can sit in the middle.
- Mounting a router that has a '/' route under a prefix fails.
- With caseSensitive: false the parameters come out in lower case.

The rules we agreed on:
- Among the routes that fit a path and a method, the most specific wins. Positions are compared from the left. At one position a static segment beats a typed parameter (int before slug), that beats a plain parameter, that beats '*', and '**' is last. If the best branch has no route for the method or does not fit further on, the next one is tried. A route for the method wins over a more specific route that lacks it.
- int is digits only. slug is lower-case letters and digits in groups joined by single dashes. A typed parameter is checked against the decoded value.
- '**' needs one or more segments. params['**'] holds them decoded and joined with '/'.
- The path is cut into segments first. A segment is then percent-decoded once; a plus sign is not a space; an encoded slash stays inside its segment and never splits it. Empty segments are dropped, '.' is dropped, '..' removes the segment before it and cannot climb above the root. A broken escape in the path gives { status: 400 }, also when no route would fit. The query string is not part of the path; the fragment is ignored.
- The query string gives an object without a prototype. A repeated key gives an array of its values in order. A plus is a space. Only the first equal sign splits a pair. A key without an equal sign has the value ''. Empty pairs are skipped. A broken escape in the query leaves that text as it is, and never fails the request.
- trailingSlash 'strict': a path with a trailing slash matches nothing (404), the root excepted. 'redirect': a trailing slash gives { status: 308, location } only when the same path without the slash would give status 200; location is the cleaned path with its segments still encoded, followed by ? and the original query string when there is one. In any other case the answer is the one for the path without the slash. 'ignore' (the default) does not care about the slash.
- Methods are not case-sensitive in add() and in match(); routes() lists them in upper case. HEAD uses a HEAD route when a route that fits has one, otherwise the GET route. A method with no route on a path that fits gives { status: 405, allow }, and OPTIONS gives { status: 204, allow } unless a route handles OPTIONS itself. allow holds every method of every route that fits the path, plus HEAD when GET is there and always OPTIONS, in alphabetical order.
- Two routes with the same method are the same route when their shapes are equal: the same static texts, parameters with the same type (names do not matter), and the same '*' and '**'. ':x?' counts as both the shorter and the longer pattern. add() throws a PatternError for such a duplicate. A parameter name may be used once in a pattern, and an optional parameter must be the last segment. A parameter that is not given leaves its name out of params.
- mount(prefix, router) adds every route of the other router under the prefix; the prefix may hold parameters and end in a slash, and '/' of the mounted router becomes the prefix itself. A route that is taken is refused as in add().
- With caseSensitive: false the static segments are compared without regard to case and the parameters keep their case.

Public exports stay as they are. The existing tests must keep passing and must not be edited; put any new tests in new files.
